title: TypeScript interfaces vs traits

writing.exampleCaption: Explicit `impl` blocks make both structs `Shape`s; `total_area` is generic, and `largest` takes trait objects.
writing.explanation:
TypeScript interfaces are structural. The object literals in the example have no `implements` clause, yet both are `Shape`s because they have `area` and `name`. Rust traits are nominal: `Square` satisfies `Shape` only after `impl Shape for Square { ... }`, and an inherent method with the same name does not count. That is the E0277 in the practice code, the trait bound `Square: Shape` is not satisfied.

A trait bound plays the role of `<T extends Shape>`. `fn total_area<T: Shape>(items: &[T])` is generic: the compiler generates a separate copy for each concrete `T` it is used with, and the calls are dispatched statically. Every item in that slice must be the same `T`, so it cannot hold a square and a rectangle together.

For a mixed collection, the counterpart of an array of interface values, use trait objects: `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>`. Each element is a pointer to some type that implements `Shape` plus a table of its methods, and calls are dispatched at runtime, which is how every JavaScript method call works anyway. Neither form is automatically faster: generics can grow code size, and trait objects add an indirection.

Traits cover other TypeScript patterns too. Default methods replace a shared base class, `impl Display for T` replaces `toString`, and implementing a standard trait such as `PartialOrd` plugs your type into existing generic code. You may implement your own trait for a foreign type such as `u32`, but not a foreign trait for a foreign type.
writing.feedback: A generic type parameter, written either way, is one concrete type per call. A slice of `Box<dyn Priced>` holds different types behind one trait.
writing.question: Which signature lets one call handle a list that mixes `Book` and `Coffee` values?

recall.answer: `User` has an inherent `name` method but no `impl Named for User`, so the bound is not satisfied: E0277. Traits are nominal. Move the method into `impl Named for User { fn name(&self) -> String { ... } }`.
recall.question: Why is the call rejected, and what fixes it?

recall.answer: When one collection must hold different concrete types, or when the type is only known at runtime. Generics fix one `T` per instantiation and are compiled into a separate copy for each; trait objects store a pointer plus a method table and dispatch at runtime. Measure before assuming either is faster.
recall.question: When is `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>` the right choice over a generic `Vec<T>` with `T: Shape`?

writing.rule: A type implements a trait only through an explicit `impl`; use a generic bound for static dispatch over one type and `dyn Trait` for a collection of mixed types.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness passes every case, including an empty list and a tie for the cheapest item. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.summary: A TypeScript interface is satisfied by any value with the right shape; a Rust trait is satisfied only by types that explicitly `impl` it.
